A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their supplied pages are readable and matchable. However, v2 refers to a full proof in Appendix A, which is absent from the supplied PDF; only its main-text proof sketch can be assessed.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, cross-architecture generalization, initialization, training-time and ablation results in Tables 1–7.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results in Tables 1–6 and adds a qualitative analysis of feature ranks in Figure 2.

M1.justification: Channel-wise sorting and joint shape/rotation optimization remain. However, Equation 8 changes the within-dataset MMD terms from ordinary kernels to sorted-feature kernels, revising the written objective. The maximum-feature loss explicitly formulated in v2 was already described in v1 Section 4.1 and its framework diagram; it is not an entirely new component. An implementation change is not established.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 3D point-cloud classification on ModelNet10, ModelNet40, ShapeNet and ScanObjectNN. The aligned, mixed and rotated dataset groupings are retained; no additional dataset, population or task is introduced.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain random selection, Herding, K-center, DC and DM, including PCC implemented as DC with Herding initialization. v2 explicitly marks that PCC correspondence in Table 3, but v1 already evaluates and identifies it in Section 4.2.2. Cross-architecture comparisons retain DC and DM.

E3.justification: The new Figure 2 introduces a probe selecting the largest, 200th-largest and 500th-largest features across 1,024 channels; the previous feature-layer comparison protocol disappears. Shared benchmark settings retain 1,024 points, PPC values 1/3/10, 1,500 distillation iterations and evaluation every 250 iterations. Omitted optimizer settings establish reduced documentation, not changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds a qualitative investigation of whether feature ranks identify semantically meaningful regions in Figure 2. It removes v1 Section 4.4.3 and Table 7, which tested feature extraction from three PointNet layers. Sorting, joint-rotation and initialization analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports mean accuracy over ten network trainings without uncertainty values. v2 retains ten trainings and first reports mean plus standard deviation throughout the main and cross-architecture comparisons in Tables 1–2. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting for the central evidence; additional runs or significance tests are not reported.

E6.justification: Several revisions exceed rounding: Table 1's proposed-method ModelNet10/PPC-3 accuracy changes from 84.96 to 84.4; Table 2's DM/DGCNN/ModelNet40 entry changes from 51.65 to 34.8, and proposed-method PointNet++/ScanObjectNN from 19.70 to 22.0. Table 5 also revises two means. v2 adds feature-rank findings and omits the layer-ablation results. Most retained results and broad rankings remain stable; these revisions do not establish an overall performance gain.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 1 and a feasible-set proof sketch showing that joint optimization cannot have a worse global minimum than shape-only optimization. It also explicitly defines the weighted full-feature/maximum-feature loss and revises the kernel terms in Equation 8. The referenced Appendix A is unavailable, so any fuller proof cannot be assessed.

C1.justification: The sorting contribution shifts from permutation-invariant feature alignment to preserving semantic correspondence between objects, changing the claimed meaning of alignment. Claims of the first distribution-matching approach for 3D point clouds, joint shape/rotation optimization, benchmark superiority and cross-architecture generalization remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets high-ranked features as identifying meaningful edges and corners, giving sorting a substantive semantic explanation. Its new limitations section acknowledges incomplete semantic alignment and discusses rotation-estimation complexity for already aligned datasets. The explanation linking deeper feature layers to increased representational capacity is removed with that ablation.

D1.justification: v1 Section 4.1 specifies SGD, learning rates of 10 for synthetic coordinates, 0.5/5 for rotation angles and 0.01 for PointNet, plus 500 PointNet training iterations. These details are absent from v2. Although v2 makes the two loss components explicit, it supplies no numerical values for their weighting parameters. Reproducibility information is substantially reduced.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 32 works and retain the same positioning against gradient, trajectory and distribution matching, including PCC. The first-distribution-matching-method novelty claim remains; bibliographic formatting and metadata changes do not alter research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, systematically replaces PIDM terminology with SADM, and extensively rewrites the abstract, motivation and method explanation. Distribution-matching background moves into Preliminaries, qualitative comparison becomes a performance-comparison subsection, and the experimental discussion is reorganized.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. The separate concept figure is removed, the framework is redrawn as Figure 1, and a new feature-rank Figure 2 appears. Table 7 disappears, Tables 1–2 become denser with uncertainty entries, and Figure 3 is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 improves statistical transparency through standard deviations in Tables 1–2, clarifies the loss formulation and adds mechanism evidence and explicit limitations. However, it removes important optimizer and training details and the feature-layer ablation, leaves loss weights unspecified, and references an absent proof appendix. These concrete gains and losses prevent a reliable net judgment of overall quality.
